A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FedLog and contain readable main text, equations, experiments, figures, tables, and appendices. The substantial revision and removal of v1's conference checklist do not prevent reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic experiments and evaluations on MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and CelebA, including communication costs, heterogeneous architectures, and differential privacy.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds FedLog-C evaluations and separate central/local differential-privacy results in Table 1 and Figure 2.

M1.justification: The original FedLog procedure is retained, but v2 introduces FedLog-C with an auxiliary loss encouraging compact, separated class representations (Eq. 15). It broadcasts aggregated statistics so clients can optimize the head locally. The DP extension also changes its noise calibration to account for multiple communication rounds.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic problem, MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and CelebA classification tasks, including heterogeneous client architectures. The changes concern method variants, client partitioning, and privacy procedures within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: The external baseline roster is unchanged. V2 adds direct comparisons between FedLog-C and the original FedLog in Table 1 and the CelebA and flexible-architecture experiments, expanding the compared variants without adding an external baseline.

E3.justification: V1 reports per-client, per-round communication and separately reports rounds to accuracy thresholds. V2 measures total communication across clients to those thresholds, stopping at peak accuracy when a threshold is never reached. CIFAR100's stated allocation changes from 2 to 10 classes per client; unchanged accuracy entries do not establish rerunning. The DP evaluation also uses revised composition-aware noise calibration and distinguishes central from local DP.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands the privacy-utility analysis from one DP curve to separate central/local DP curves under revised accounting. FedLog-C versus FedLog comparisons examine the added clustering loss, including its behavior with heterogeneous architectures. The original synthetic representation analysis remains.

E5.justification: Six synthetic seeds, ten benchmark seeds, accuracy standard errors, plotted standard deviations, and one-tailed Wilcoxon tests are retained. The statistical reference changes from FedLog to FedLog-C, and the revised total-communication comparisons include uncertainty and significance annotations. No increase in run counts is reported.

E6.justification: Existing Table 1 accuracy values are retained, while FedLog-C adds 98.41%, 87.57%, and 56.78% on MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100, plus 71.96% on CelebA and 55.86% with flexible architectures. Total-cost results replace per-round costs; several reproduce v1's costs multiplied by client counts and convergence rounds. Under revised DP accounting, v2 reports near-optimal central-DP accuracy at epsilon at least 0.5 and acceptable local-DP accuracy at least 5, replacing v1's single-curve conclusion at 0.1.

T1.justification: V2 adds Theorem 2 and Appendix B's definitions and proof that the shared statistic is minimal sufficient and independent of ancillary statistics under the stated model. Its privacy theorem and Appendix C replace single-release Gaussian calibration with a k-round adaptive-composition result and expanded derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract strengthens the characterization of shared summaries from sufficient to minimal sufficient statistics. The headline communication claim changes from as little as 1.6% per round to 0.09% of FedAvg's total communication. This redefines the claimed efficiency measure rather than establishing a directly comparable reduction between versions.

C2.justification: V2 replaces the characterization of the Gaussian-feature assumption as mild with a mismatch that FedLog-C seeks to mitigate. It explicitly limits the method to classification and distinguishes trusted-server/MPC privacy utility from local DP. Conversely, v1's explicit warning that predictive posteriors and the prior normalizer remain intractable is omitted.

D1.justification: V2 adds an O(m*nclass) complexity statement for head optimization. Hardware, preprocessing, network architectures, hyperparameter Tables A.2–A.4, and the supplementary-code statement remain unchanged. The new FedLog-C loss weights are defined but their experimental values are not supplied.

R1.justification: V2 emphasizes federated representation learning and adds references supporting representation learning, contrastive learning, sufficiency, and privacy composition, including Liu et al., Schroff et al., Casella and Berger, Koopman, and Kairouz et al. Existing related work is retained, with communication-efficient and Bayesian FL discussions moved to Appendix A.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around representation learning. Background material is reorganized into related work and model construction, mathematical explanations are expanded, and a dedicated Limitations section is added. Appendices are reorganized and the NeurIPS checklist is removed.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from one-column to two-column layout. Table 1 is expanded and replaces the separate communication/convergence presentation. V1's Figures 2 and 3 become a stacked Figure 2 with additional method and privacy curves; CelebA example photographs are removed. Appendix tables are also reformatted and relocated.

improvement.justification: V2 improves the treatment of privacy through multi-round accounting and explicit central/local distinctions, and better states applicability limits. FedLog-C adds useful comparative evidence. However, its loss weights remain undocumented, Eq. 15 ambiguously subtracts m-dimensional class means from m*nclass-dimensional statistics, and existing CIFAR100 scores accompany a changed stated partition. These technical and reproducibility gaps limit the overall gain; the smaller communication headline also uses a different metric.
